sub_skills: Predicting outcomes and making reasoned decisions
Working with others to generate ideas
Looking for patterns and making generalisation
Talking confidently and explaining ideas/opinions clearly
Using a range of media to communicate ideas
Using mathematics to justify and support decisions
Using technology to create, manipulate and process information
Using technology to collaborate, communicate and refine work
Respectfully responding to people of all cultures
Appreciating ethnicity as a cradle for creativity and innovation

values: Honesty, uphold and defend the truth at all times
Justice and fairness in dealing with others
Integrity; moral uprightness and sound character

themes.theme_description: Mechanics (Circular Motion, SHM, Gravitation) and Waves (Progressive, Stationary, Sound)

topics.core_competency: The learner examines the motion of bodies on curved paths and ensures safety precautions for people using automobiles on such paths.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: investigate the forces acting on bodies moving in circular paths and how they relate to safety. (u, s, gs, v/a)
derive the expressions for motion under conical pendulum and apply them in real life. (u, s, v/a)
investigate the conditions for non-skidding on banked and horizontal roads to ensure safety. (u, v/a)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Motion in a vertical circle should not be included.

suggested_learning_activities.description: In a discussion and brainstorming session, learners identify daily life situations where motion in a circle exists and make presentations
In groups, learners explain the meaning of the terms; angular velocity, angular acceleration and centripetal force.
In groups, learners research and derive expressions for angular velocity, angular acceleration and centripetal force, and use them in solving related numerical problems.
In pairs, learners review, brainstorm, discuss and make presentations on the effect of gravity on the motion of bodies in a circular path.
Learners research, discuss and make presentations on expressions for the conical pendulum and apply them in solving numerical problems.
In a discussion and brainstorming session, learners identify daily life situations where motion on banked roads exists and make presentations.

In groups, learners explain the meaning of angle of banking and derive expressions relating the angle of banking, velocity and acceleration of bodies moving in a circular path and apply these expressions in solving numerical problems.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ presentations while looking for appropriateness in: i) application of circular motion in daily life situations; and ii) derivations of the expressions under circular motion and their use in solving numerical problems.
Assess learners’ products on the coherence and quality of write-ups in (a) above.
Observe learners’ participation and listen to their discussion while looking for accuracy of information and correcting any misconceptions.
Dialogue with learners while assessing their ability to correctly: i) derive the expressions for the motion on the conical pendulum; and ii) use the expressions to solve numerical problems.
Assess leaners’ product on the coherence and correctness of the write-ups in (b) above.

Observe learners’ presentations while looking for: i) correct conditions for non-skidding motion on a circular path; and ii) correct derivations of the expressions under banked motion and their use in solving numerical problems.
Assess learners’ products on the coherence and quality of write-ups in (a) above.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Motion in a vertical circle should not be included.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the behaviour of oscillating systems in order to optimise the performance of devices that employ simple harmonic motion.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: explain terminologies used in simple harmonic motion (SHM) and apply them to oscillating systems. (u, s)
explore energy conservation in oscillating systems and its implications in various daily experiences. (u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on the derivations of expressions of displacement, velocity, acceleration, energy, period and frequency of a body executing SHM and apply the expressions to solve numerical problems.

Learners in groups discuss and make presentations on the oscillations of; simple pendulum, floating cylinder, liquid in a U-tube, mass at the end of a vertical spring or a horizontal spring on a smooth surface and derive expressions to show that these oscillations execute SHM.
In groups or as individuals, learners use the expressions derived in (b) above to solve related numerical problems.

Learners in groups discuss the applications of SHM in the determination of acceleration due to gravity, g and other real-life situations such as shock absorbers, guitars, diving boards, earthquake proofs in buildings, to mention but a few.

In pairs, learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) interchange of energy in a SHM and relate it to the principle of conservation of energy; and ii) different types of oscillations and their implications in real life.
Learners work in groups to model and design oscillating system devices.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe and assess the presentations of learners while looking for: i) correctness of concepts, terminologies and graphical representation of SHM; and ii) characteristics of SHM.

Dialogue with learners to find out the correctness and coherence in: i) experimental determination of acceleration due to gravity; ii) derivation of expressions for bodies executing SHM; and iii) solving numerical problems.

Assess learners: i) on logical reasoning and acceptance of constructive criticism in their discussions about the applications of SHM in real-life situations; and ii) on the correctness of their write-ups.
Observe and assess the presentations of learners while looking for correctness of concepts of energy conversions in different oscillating systems and graphical representations.

Dialogue with learners while assessing: i) the accuracy and relevance of the implications of the different types of oscillations in real life; and ii) choice of materials suitable for the construction of the selected system.
Assess learners’ products while looking for creativity, innovation, teamwork and workability of the model.

topics.core_competency: The learner evaluates the effects of gravitation and its applications on objects both on earth and in space.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply the laws and principles of gravitation to real life. (u, v/a, gs)
investigate the effect of gravity on bodies orbiting in space such as communication satellites and related phenomena. (u, s, gs)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Experimental determination of G should be left out.

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) the interaction of masses in space and the nature of force acting on them; ii) Kepler’s and Newton’s laws of gravitation; and iii) gravitational field intensity.
Learners use the information from activity (a) above to derive the dimensions and S.I units of the gravitational constant, G.

In groups learners use Newton’s and Kepler’s laws of gravitation to explain and derive the expressions for: i) the variations of g with latitude; ii) weightlessness in orbits; and iii) distance of bodies from the centre of the earth and how it relates to ocean tides, seasons, cyclones among others, and make presentations.
As individuals or in groups, learners use the expressions derived in (c) above to solve related numerical problems.
Learners use Kepler’s and Newton’s laws of gravitation to determine parking orbits, velocity of escape and energy of the satellite.
Learners review previous knowledge about satellites and their applications in; communication (telephone, television, radio broadcast), navigation, disaster management and security among others.
Learners use ICT tools such as simulations and videos to study orbiting satellites and planets, and make presentations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners as they present about Kepler’s and Newton’s laws of gravitation while assessing their ability to: i) effectively express themselves and respect others’ opinions; ii) use a range of presentation techniques; and iii) explain the implications of the laws.

Assess the learners’ written products about Kepler’s and Newton’s laws on gravitation while looking for: i) accuracy in statements of the laws; and ii) correct use of mathematical expressions to solve numerical problems and explain related phenomena.

Observe and probe learners during the presentations while assessing their ability to: i) determine parking orbits, velocity of escape and energy of the satellite in orbit; and ii) confidently explain the applications of satellites in real life.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) logical flow in the derivation of expressions describing the motion of bodies in orbits around the earth; ii) accuracy in the determination of parking orbits, velocity of escape and energy of satellites; and iii) relevancy and coherence in applications of satellites.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Experimental determination of G should be left out.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the propagation of progressive waves in matter and its application in different situations.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: deduce that waves are a means of transferring energy and that this has many applications. (u, s, gs)
deduce that when waves interfere, they generate properties that have various applications in real life. (u, s, gs, v/a)
explain concepts related to diffraction of waves and apply them to everyday life situations. (s, gs, v/a)
examine the phenomenon of wave polarisation and how it applies to real life. (u, v/a)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Numerical concepts on polarisation of light should be left out.

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners review, brainstorm, discuss and make presentations about: i) terminologies used in waves; ii) types and forms of waves; iii) the general wave equation; iv) reflection and refraction of waves.

In groups, learners research, explain and report on: i) the characteristics of a progressive wave and state their examples; and ii) different types of wave fronts, optical path, reflection and refraction of waves and phases of vibration.

In groups, learners research and derive the expression for displacement on a progressive wave; y = a sin 2π(t/T ± x/λ) and explain the significance of ± in the equation, and use it to solve numerical problems.
In pairs, learners research, discuss and make presentations on Huygen’s principle and its application in a variety of situations.
Learners model and develop communication systems that use the concept of progressive wave transmission.

Learners review, brainstorm, discuss and make presentations about: i) the term interference of waves; ii) the conditions for constructive and destructive interference to occur; and iii) production of interference in a ripple tank.

In groups, learners research and report on: i) coherent sources, path difference, energy of a wave, division of amplitude and wavefront; ii) Young’s double slit experiment and derive the expression Δy = λD/a and how it is applied to solve numerical problems; and iii) appearance of fringes and how Young’s double slit experiment can be used for measuring wavelength, slit separation, and fringe separation.

Learners in groups research, discuss and make presentations on: i) the concept of diffraction of waves; ii) the dependence of diffraction on wavelength; iii) derive the expression dsinθ = nλ for diffraction of waves and use it to solve numerical problems; and iv) the occurrence of diffraction in real life.
Learners describe the appearance of diffraction images in a single slit, double slit and discuss the effect of the number of slits per unit length on the appearance of fringes.

In groups, learners research, discuss and report about: i) concept of polarisation of light; ii) distinction between plane polarised and non-plane polarised light; iii) polaroid; iv) production of polarised light using a variety of methods; and v) applications of polarised light.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ presentations and look out for: i) the correctness of the meanings of terminologies and correct any misconceptions; and ii) individual learner’s participation.

Converse with learners while asking probing questions to test their ability to: i) identify the types of progressive waves; ii) represent reflection and refraction of progressive waves using appropriate diagrams; and iii) explain the significance of ± in the progressive wave equation.

Assess products while looking for: i) correctness of the meanings of terminologies related to progressive waves; ii) coherence in the derivation of the progressive wave equation and its proper use in substitution; and iii) innovations and creativity in the development of models.
Observe learners’ presentations while assessing: i) the correctness of the meanings of interference of waves and its applications; and ii) individual learner’s participation.

Probe learners’ ability to: i) relate amplitude, frequency, velocity and phase during the superposition of different waves; and ii) identify the conditions for constructive and destructive interference and correct any misconceptions.
Asses learners’ written products basing on the ability to: i) draw and explain fringe patterns in different situations; and ii) describe the young’s experiment coherently.
Observe learners’ discussions while assessing their ability to: i) participate and relate; and ii) correctness of the terms, concepts and sketch diagrams.

Assess written products while looking for ability to: i) relate atomic spacing to optical; ii) path length for diffraction in a material; and iii) explain the applications of diffraction in different situations.

Observe learners’ presentations and look out for the correctness and accuracy of the meanings of terms and concepts related to polarisation (polariser, transmission axis, s and p polarised waves) and correct any misconceptions.
Converse with learners paying particular attention to their ability to explain the concept of polarisation and distinguish between polarised and unpolarised light and correct any misconceptions.
Assess written products while looking for: i) coherence in the process of production of polarised light by different methods; and ii) applications of polarised light.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Numerical concepts on polarisation of light should be left out.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the behaviour of stationary waves and their applications in different situations.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse the behaviour of stationary waves, and the expressions that describe them. (u, s)
deduce that stationary waves can be produced in pipes and strings for use in a variety of situations.
illustrate the concept of resonance of waves and its applications. (u, s, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners research, discuss and present on: i) the superposition of progressive waves; ii) formation and characteristics of stationary waves stating examples; and iii) derivation of the stationary wave equation and its use in solving numerical problems.

In groups, learners research, discuss and report on: i) stationary waves on stretched strings; ii) factors affecting the pitch of a note from a stretched string; iii) derivation of the expression v = √(T/μ) and use it to solve numerical problems; iv) stationary waves in pipes and determine end-error-correction; and v) harmonics in strings and pipes and how they relate to the advantages and disadvantages of open and closed pipes.
In groups, learners investigate how frequency is determined in a stretched string.
In groups or as individuals, learners model systems that apply the concept of stationary waves in pipes and strings.
In groups, learners research, discuss and present on: i) resonance in strings and pipes (closed and open); and ii) how resonance relates to the length of an air column in a pipe or length of string.
In groups, learners determine the speed of sound in air using a resonance tube.
Learners discuss and report on applications of stationary waves in electronics such as radio, TV receivers, amplifiers and filters.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe the discussions and presentations while assessing the correctness of superposition and characteristics of stationary waves.
Probe learners while assessing their ability to explain the formation of stationary waves and their features.
Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) coherency in the derivation of the stationary wave equation; and ii) proper application of the equation to solve numerical problems.

Probe learners while assessing their ability to: i) identify points of maximum and minimum energy on a stationary wave; ii) establish resonance positions and end corrections; and iii) solve numerical problems relating to wavelengths, velocity and frequency in a stationary wave.

Assess written products while focussing on: i) coherency in the derivation of velocity in a stationary wave; ii) coherence in the steps used to investigate how frequency in stretched strings is determined; and iii) workability and innovation in the models of learners.

Converse with learners to ascertain whether they can explain the application of stationary waves: i) to control the quality and pitch of sound; ii) in production of beats and reverberations in amplifiers; and iii) in resonance to explain the tuning of radio, amplifiers and TV.

Assess written products to ascertain the: i) appropriateness of the materials (strings, masses) and the procedures used in the investigation; ii) appropriateness and use of the materials (tuning forks of different frequencies metre rule) in investigating resonance; iii) proper use of wave equation in determining the speed of sound using resonance; and iv) identification of possible sources of errors in the investigation and how they can be minimised.

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates the behaviour of sound waves and their applications in different situations.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: analyse beats, notes and octaves as applied in sound, and their implications in a variety of situations. (u, s)
investigate doppler effect and how it applies to various fields. (u, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners review in a think-pair-share session and discuss: i) the production and propagation of sound in different media; ii) factors that affect the speed of sound in different media; iii) echoes and reverberations; and iv) methods of determining the speed of sound.
Learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) the meaning of tone, fundamental note, overtones, harmonics, octaves, and beats; and ii) the effect of overtones on the quality of sound.

In groups, learners research and discuss on: i) formation of beats and their applications; and ii) derivation of the expression for beat frequency Δf = f2 - f1 and apply it in solving numerical problems.

Learners in groups research, discuss and make presentations about description of some applications of doppler effect such as sonar, weather forecasting, tracking systems, sirens, radar, medical imaging, blood flow and satellite communication.
In groups, learners research and make models of cell phones, radio broadcasting or sound scan imaging among others that use the concept of waves in their mode of operation.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ discussion and look out for the correctness and accuracy of the concepts relating to the: i) production and propagation of sound in different media; and ii) formation of overtones and harmonics and correct any misconceptions.

Dialogue with learners while looking for: i) understanding of how beats are formed and correcting any misconceptions; ii) applications of beats in real-life situations; and iii) correct procedure used in the derivation.

Assess written products and ascertain the: i) correctness in the terminologies related to sound waves; ii) coherence in the derivation of beat frequency; and iii) application of the beat frequency expression.

Observe the presentations in order while assessing the learners’: i) understanding of the concept of doppler effect; ii) ability to derive the equations of frequency in different relative motions and proper use of wave equations in the investigation of doppler effect; iii) ability to explain the theory of different systems based on the doppler effect; and iv) understanding of echoes, reverberations and interference of sound waves.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) coherence in derivation of the apparent frequency in doppler effect and its use; ii) proper statements for application of doppler effect; and iii) innovations in the models made by learners.

themes.theme_description: Current Electricity, Magnetism, Magnetic Effects, Induction, and A.C. Circuits

topics.core_competency: The learner investigates electric current, it’s properties, transmission and uses in order to reduce power losses and improve personal and national safety.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: deduce the relationship between current, resistance and voltage, and how they relate to transmission of charges in materials. (u, s)
investigate the operation of slide wire meters and apply them in a variety of situations. (s, gs, v, a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In a brainstorming session, learners make review, discuss and report on: i) electric current, emf, resistance and potential difference, internal resistance, Ohm’s law and its verification; and ii) effective resistance for resistors in series and parallel arrangements and solve related numerical problems.
In groups, learners research, investigate and report on: ii) heating effects of electric current; and iii) resistivity and temperature coefficient of resistance of a material.

In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) expressions for electric energy and power; and ii) derivation for the condition for maximum power output in an Ohmic resistor and sketch graphs for variation of efficiency, power output and terminal potential difference (p.d) with load resistance.
In pairs, learners research, discuss and present on Kirchhoff’s laws and use them to solve electrical circuit problems.
In groups, learners explain the use of resistors in the modification of galvanometers into ammeters and voltmeters.
In groups, learners review the operation of a potential divider and make presentations during plenary.
In groups, learners search, discuss and make presentations on the mode of operation and solve numerical problems relating to the: i) Wheatstone bridge. ii) Meter bridge. iii) Potentiometer.
In groups, learners investigate how the slide wire meters are used to measure: i) resistance and internal resistance. ii) emf and p.d across a resistor. iii) electric current.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ participation while looking for: i) accurate information about electric current, emf, resistance and potential difference and their units; and ii) correct statement of Ohm’s law its mathematical expression, graphical interpretations while correcting any misconceptions.

Discuss with learners during their presentations while looking for: i) correct meaning of resistivity and temperature coefficient of resistance; ii) accurate explanations of the heating effect of electric current; iii) how resistance, cross-section area and length of the wire affects the efficiency of power transmission; and iv) why long-distance transmission requires low current.

Assess written products to ascertain the: i) logical flow of procedures and deductions made during the investigation of internal resistance; ii) appropriateness of the procedures used in the derivation of the maximum power; iii) ability to sketch graphs of efficiency, power output and p.d with load; iv) ability to resolve resistor networks using Kirchhoff’s laws; and v) correctness of explanations relating to the conversion of galvanometers into ammeters and voltmeters.

Observe learners’ presentations to ascertain: i) active participation; ii) correct explanation about the operation of potential dividers; and iii) appropriateness of the materials selected for investigation.

Assess learners’ written products while emphasising the: i) ability of the learners to describe the operation of a slide wire potentiometer and establishment of calibration constant; and ii) learners’ ability to manipulate data to determine resistance, emf of cell and emf of thermocouples, and current.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates the magnetic properties of matter and uses them to model different useful magneto-electric devices.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: deduce that the Earth has magnetic properties and this has many implications. (u, s, gs)
explain how magnetisation and demagnetisation occur in matter. (u, s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In a brainstorming session, learners review and report on the following: i) magnetic fields and magnetic field lines, neutral point, magnetic shielding; and ii) Earth’s magnetic field.

In pairs, learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) geographic and magnetic meridian, magnetic and geographic axes, angle of dip, declination, horizontal and vertical components of the Earth’s field; and ii) magnetic flux and magnetic flux density B, deduce its expression and unit; and apply it to solve numerical problems.
In a brainstorming session, learners review and give a report on the domain theory, magnetisation, magnetic saturation and demagnetisation, using molecular theory.

In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) the features of the graphs showing the variation of B with the magnetic field strength, H; and ii) characteristics of hard and soft magnetic materials, ferromagnetic, paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials.
In groups, learners model devices that show the practical uses of magnetism in matter.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ presentations while looking for: i) accuracy of information about the neutral point, magnetic shielding and the Earth’s magnetic fields with clear drawings, and correct any misconceptions; and ii) correct sketches of magnetic field patterns for different magnet arrangements.

Assess learners’ written products while considering the: i) correctness of the meanings of terminologies relating to Earth’s magnetic field; and ii) logical flow of the derivation of flux density and its use in solving related numerical problems.

Discuss with learners during their presentations while looking for: i) correct understanding of domain theory and magnetic saturation; and ii) learners’ ability to explain magnetisation and demagnetisation using molecular theory.

Evaluate learners’ products while considering: i) the correctness of the graphs of variation of B and H, its features; ii) correct characteristics of hard and soft magnetic materials, ferromagnetic, paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials; and iii) workability of the modelled devices and their relevance to society.

topic_metadata.topic_title: MAGNETIC EFFECT OF AN ELECTRIC CURRENT

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates that a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force and uses this concept to design models of different devices to solve societal needs.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: investigate the existence of a force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. (u, s, gs,)
use Biot-Savart’s law to write expressions for magnetic flux density in a variety of situations. (u, s, gs)
explain how the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is applied in the operation of various electrical devices. (u, s)

explicitly_excluded.text_verbatim: Experiments to measure B along a straight conductor, centre of circular coil and solenoid are not required.

suggested_learning_activities.description: In a brainstorming session, learners review, discuss and make presentations on the following: i) magnetic fields around current carrying conductors; ii) direction of the force on current carrying conductor in a magnetic field; and iii) factors affecting the magnitude of the force on current carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

In groups or as individuals, learners derive the expressions: F = BIlsinθ for the force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field F = Bqvsinθ for the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field.
Use the expressions for the forces above to solve related numerical problems.

In a think-pair-share, learners research, discuss and make presentations about: i) the expression for Biot-Savart’s law and interpret it; ii) the expressions for flux density at a perpendicular distance from a straight conductor, at the centre of a coil and in a solenoid; iii) use of the expression; F = BIlsinθ to determine the expression for the magnetic force between two long parallel current carrying conductors; iv) the Hall effect hence derive an expression for the Hall voltage VH = BI/net; v) the use of expressions to solve related numerical problems.
In a class discussion, learners derive the expression for the torque on a coil in a magnetic field τ = BANIsinθ and use it to solve related numerical problems.

In group projects, learners fabricate devices such as an electric bell, a loudspeaker, a simple d.c motor and any others that use the concept of a force and torque around a current carrying conductor.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners during the presentations while assessing: i) participation and effective communication; ii) proper sketches of magnetic fields on straight conductors, coils, magnets and solenoids; iii) methods used to investigate the force existing on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field; and iv) the correctness of the factors affecting this force.

Probe learners while assessing their ability to: i) explain how the force on a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field can be varied; and ii) describe the applications of this force in devices like d.c motor, relay and others.

Assess written products while emphasising: i) coherence in the derivations of forces on conductors and charges in a magnetic field and the use of the equations in solving numerical problems; and ii) proper sketches of magnetic fields in different situations.

Observe learners during the discussions while assessing: i) how learners can interpret the expressions for Biot-savart’s law and apply them; ii) the correctness of the expressions for flux density at a perpendicular distance from a straight conductor, at the centre of a coil and in a solenoid and the use made of them; and iii) the logical flow in the derivation of the force between two long conductors carrying current.

Converse with learners to ascertain whether they can: i) apply the expression for the force between two long conductors carrying current to define an ampere; and ii) describe the Hall effect and its derivation.
Discuss with learners while assessing how they explain the torque in electromagnetic devices and apply the expression for torque to solve numerical problems.

Assess learners’ products while considering: i) the workability of the devices that use the principle of force in a current carrying conductor in a magnetic field; ii) the correctness of the write-ups describing the operation of the devices above; and iii) the correctness of derivation of torque on a coil in a magnetic field and the proper substitutions used to solve numerical problems.

syllabus_notes.text_verbatim: Experiments to measure B along a straight conductor, centre of circular coil and solenoid are not required.

topics.core_competency: The learner evaluates how magnetism and current are linked and how this principle is applied in the operation of transformers and generators.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: explain the concept of electromagnetic induction and how it is applied in a variety of situations. (u, s, gs)
appreciate the concepts of self and mutual induction and their application in a variety of devices. (u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners review, brainstorm, discuss and make presentation on the use of a coil and a magnet to demonstrate the production of electricity; and use Fleming’s right-hand rule to determine direction of the induced current.

In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) magnetic flux linkage; ii) Induced emf; iii) relationship between the change in flux linkage and induced current; iv) statements for the laws of electromagnetic induction; v) derivation for the expressions of Faraday’s and Lenz’s laws; and vi) using the derived expressions to solve numerical problems.

In groups, learners review, brainstorm, discuss and make presentations on the: i) concepts of mutual and self-induction; ii) mode of operation of d.c and a.c generators; and iii) mode of operation of a transformer and its efficiency.

In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on the: i) derivations of the expressions for mutual and self-induction and apply them to solve numerical problems; ii) explanation of the processes that lead to the production of a back e.m.f and eddy currents in a motor coil; iii) derivation of the expressions for back e.m.f and eddy currents, and their applications; and iv) structure and mode of operation of moving coil meters.
In groups, learners carry out project works to model devices that employ the principles of electromagnetic induction.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Dialogue with learners while looking for their: i) choice of materials used in demonstrating electromagnetic induction; ii) understanding of how electricity is produced in a conductor by a changing magnetic flux; and iii) ability to use Fleming’s right-hand rule to determine the direction of the current.

Assess learners’ written products while considering the: i) correctness of the statements of the laws of electromagnetic induction and related concepts. ii) correct application of Faraday’s and Lenz’s laws in solving numerical problems.
Observe group presentations while emphasising: i) proper illustrations of the direction of current; and ii) correctness of concepts about electromagnetic induction.

Converse with learners during their presentations while looking for: i) correct understanding of how a change in flux linkage induces current in a conductor; ii) correctness of procedures of derivations based on the assumptions made; and iii) correct understanding of how a.c and d.c generators operate, and how back e.m.f is produced.

Assess products while looking for the: i) correct explanation of how eddy currents are produced in coils; ii) correct statements for the concept of self and mutual induction, and the procedure used; iii) coherence in the derivation of expression for eddy currents and back e.m.f.; and iv) selection of materials for the models, their innovativeness, creativity and workability of the models.

topics.core_competency: The learner measures a.c and investigates its behaviour in different devices.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: explain the operation of a.c measuring devices and their various applications in real life. (u, s)
evaluate the inductance, reactance and impedance of a.c circuits and their applications in real life. (u, s, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners review, brainstorm, discuss and make presentations on the: i) meaning of a.c and d.c and how they can be interconverted; and ii) advantage of using a.c in commercial supply compared to d.c.

In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on the: i) structure and mode of operation of the hot wire meter and moving iron meter; ii) the meaning of root mean square value (rms) of current/voltage, and the peak value of a.c; and iii) derivation of the expressions for rms of current and voltage and their use in solving numerical problems.

In groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) effect of capacitors and inductors in a.c circuits; ii) derivation of expressions for inductive and capacitive reactances; iii) derivation of expressions for impedance in a.c series circuits and solve related numerical problems; iv) the average energy and power in a resistor, capacitor and inductor connected separately in an ac circuit; v) the use of the derived expressions to solve numerical problems; and vi) characteristic graphs for a.c flowing through a resistor (R), capacitor (C) and inductor (L) connected individually and in combinations.
In groups, learners research and model simple electronic devices using capacitors, inductors and resistors arranged in a circuit board and explain how they work.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe and evaluate the learners’ presentations based on: i) the ability to distinguish between a.c and d.c and how they can be interconverted; and ii) the understanding of the advantages of using a.c in commercial power supply compared to d.c.
Converse with learners and probe their understanding of the operation of a hot wire meter and moving iron meter.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) correct description of the operation of hot wire meters and moving iron meters; and ii) correct meaning of root mean square value, its derivation and application in solving numerical problems.
Observe learners during the presentations while assessing their ability to: i) communicate effectively; and ii) logically present ideas during the derivation of reactances and impedances.

Discuss with learners while assessing their ability to: i) explain the steps in the derivations of combined resistance; ii) correctly interpret the sketch graphs and phasor diagrams; and iii) explain the effect of L, R and C on the flow of a.c current in a circuit.

Assess learners’ products while looking for: i) correct description of the effects of capacitors and inductors in circuits; ii) logical flow of the derivations for energy and power in a.c circuits; iii) coherent explanation of the a.c graphs; and iv) workability and innovation in the modelled electronic devices.

themes.theme_description: Atomic Particles, Quantum Theory, and Nuclear Processes

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates the structure of the atom and how the components of the atom are applied in different devices.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: apply the Rutherford’s scattering experiment to explain atomic structure. (s, u)
examine the behaviour of charged particles and their applications in real life. (u, s, gs)

suggested_learning_activities.description: Learners review, brainstorm and make presentations on Dalton’s atomic theory, the particles constituting an atom and their properties.

As groups, learners research, discuss and make presentations on: i) the procedure of Rutherford’s scattering experiment and the observations therein; and ii) the conclusions made from Rutherford’s experiment in terms of the structure of atoms.
As groups, learners discuss Millikan’s oil drop and Thomson’s experiments to determine electronic charge, specific charge and explain charge quantisation.
In groups, learners search and discuss the mass spectrometer and how it can be used to determine the specific charge of positive ions.

In class discussion, learners research and make presentations on: i) production of cathode rays and positive rays in a cathode ray tube; ii) characteristics that distinguish cathode and positive rays; and iii) derive expressions for the motion of electrons in electric and magnetic fields and apply them in solving numerical problems.
In groups, learners explore qualitatively the deflection of electron and ion beams through electric and magnetic fields and discuss the observed pattern.
In plenary, learners discuss the applications of cathode rays in real life.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Dialogue with learners while looking for their: i) ability to recall the fundamental particles in atoms; ii) ability to explain the Rutherford’s scattering experiment; and iii) understanding of the Rutherford’s model of an atom.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) correctness of explanation of the Millikan’s oil drop experiment, and how it can be used to determine specific charge; ii) coherent explanation about how the mass spectrometer can be used to determine the specific charge; and iii) correct derivations of relevant expressions and their use in solving numerical problems.

Observe learners’ participation in the discussions while looking for: i) accuracy of information about the production and properties of cathode rays and positive rays; and ii) proper use of sketches in explaining the production and deflection of cathode rays in electric and magnetic field.
In a conversation, probe learners to ascertain whether: i) they can account for the observed path of particles in electric and magnetic fields; and ii) distinguish cathode rays from positive rays.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) correct write-ups for the procedure of producing cathode rays and positive rays; ii) coherent derivation of the path taken by electrons in a magnetic and electric field; and iii) proper substitutions while solving numerical problems.

topics.core_competency: The learner examines how electromagnetic waves carry energy in packets and that this behaviour can be harnessed in a variety of fields.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: explain the process of photoelectric effect and its applications in real life. (u, gs)
analyse Bohr’s model and how it is used to explain atomic spectra of different elements. (u, s, gs)
deduce that when fast moving electrons are stopped by matter, they produce energetic radiations which have many applications. (u, s, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: In groups, learners research, discuss and present on the: i) meaning of photoelectric effect and its characteristics; and ii) explanation of photoelectric emission using quantum theory.

Learners report on the results of their discussion on the: i) description of the experiment to verify Einstein’s photoelectric effect and determination of the Plank’s constant; ii) Einstein’s photoelectric equation; and iii) ½MV²max = hf - ϕ, and its application in solving related numerical problems.
Learners use the theory of photoelectric effect to model burglar alarms, photocell, photo sensors, among others.
In groups, learners review, discuss and present on inadequacies of Rutherford’s atomic model.

In groups, learners research, discuss and report on Bohr’s model of the atom and use it to explain the: i) origin of absorption and emission spectra; ii) presence of energy levels in atoms; and iii) ionisation in atoms and calculate ionisation energy.
In groups, learners review, discuss and present on the production, characteristics, uses and health hazards of X-rays.

In groups, learners research, discuss and report on: i) types of X-rays; ii) continuous (background) radiation, line X-ray spectra and cut-off wavelength; iii) derivation of the expression hc/λmin = eV and its application in solving numerical problems; and iv) diffraction of X-rays, derivation of Bragg’s law 2dsinθ = nλ and application of the equation in different situations.
Learners watch videos or simulations showing motion of electrons to produce X-rays and interpret them.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners’ group presentations while assessing: i) correct description of the quantum theory of electromagnetic radiations; ii) correct explanation of the photoelectric effect based on quantum theory; and iii) participation of individual learners.
Dialogue with learners about the: i) significance of the photo electric equation; and ii) procedures used to verify Einstein’s equation and hence determination of Plank’s constant.

Assess learners’ products while emphasising: i) correct meaning of photoelectric effect, work function and related terminologies; ii) logical flow of derivation of photoelectric effect equation and its implications; iii) logical flow of the determination of Plank’s constant; and iv) innovativeness, creativity and workability of the models that employ photoelectric effect principles.

Converse with learners during their presentations while looking for: i) correct understanding of the inadequacies Rutherford’s model; ii) correct description of Bohr’s model of the atom; iii) correct procedure used in the derivation of energy of an electron; and iv) correct illustration and interpretation of energy levels of an atom.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) correct statements in the Bohr’s model of the atom; ii) coherence in the description of the origins of atomic spectra and their significance; and iii) correct use of the expressions for calculating ionisation energies.

Observe learners’ participation while looking for: i) accuracy of information about the structure and operation of the X-ray tube; and ii) correct statements about the properties of X-rays, their uses and health hazards of X-rays to humans.

Discuss with learners while looking for: i) understanding of the concept of diffraction by crystals, diffraction planes, atomic spacing, conditions for Bragg’s law; and ii) the understanding of the origin of the energy of the X-ray radiation.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) coherence in the description of the production of X-rays; ii) logical flow in the derivations of energy of X-rays and Bragg’s law and their applications; and iii) distinction between soft and hard X-rays.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates that nuclear reactions involve high amounts of energy which can be both constructive and destructive.

learning_outcomes.outcome_text: appreciate that nuclear reactions generate energy which can be harnessed for different purposes. (u, s, v/a)
deduce that nuclides disintegrate emitting particles and energy which have a variety of applications. (u, s, gs, v/a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: As a class, learners review and brainstorm the: i) meanings of nuclide, atomic number, mass number and isotopes and give examples; and ii) meaning of nuclear fission and nuclear fusion and represent them using equations.

In groups, learners research, discuss and report on: i) the meaning of unified atomic mass unit and its equivalent in electron volts; ii) Einstein’s mass-energy relation ΔE = Δmc²; iii) binding energy, mass defect and binding energy per nucleon; iv) factors which affect nuclear stability; v) the graph to study the variation of binding energy per nucleon with mass number and its significance on nuclear fission and fusion processes; vi) production of electrical energy using nuclear processes; and vii) derivation of expressions under nuclear energy and use them to solve numerical problem.
Learners debate the merits and demerits of using nuclear energy in real life.
Learners watch a video showing nuclear fusion and fission and compare them.

In groups, learners review, discuss and present on: i) the meaning of radioactivity, radiations emitted during radioactivity, their properties and balanced equations for nuclear equations; ii) the meaning of Half-life and its determination using the graphical method; and iii) uses, hazards and safety precautions of nuclear radiations.
In pairs, learners describe the structure and mode of operation of radiation detection devices (ionisation chamber, Geiger Müller tube and counter, cloud chamber) and make presentations.

In groups, learners discuss and present on: i) the law of radioactivity, the decay constant; ii) derivation of the expression N = N₀e^(-λt) and use it to deduce the expression for half-life; then apply them in solving numerical problems; and iii) use of decay equations to estimate the age of fossils and rocks.
In groups, learners research and discuss the production of artificial isotopes (induced radioactivity), their applications and make presentations.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: Observe learners during the brainstorming session while assessing: i) levels of participation, communication, creativity and innovation; and ii) ability of learners to correctly explain the meaning of mass number, atomic number, isotopes, nuclear fission and fusion.
Dialogue with learners while checking for their understanding of the process of generation of electricity using nuclear reactions; the merits and demerits of this source of electricity.

Assess learners’ written products while emphasising the: i) correct statement for meaning of atomic mass unit (U), and its relation with electron volt, joules and kilogram; ii) correct method of calculating the mass defect and energy released during a nuclear reaction; iii) sketch of a graph of B.E per nucleon against mass number and its accurate description; and iv) accurate description of the factors that affect nuclear stability.
Observe learners’ participation while looking for accuracy of information about the types and properties of the radiations emitted during radioactivity and correct any misconceptions.

Discuss with learners to ascertain the: i) correct meaning of radioactivity, types and properties of the radiations emitted during radioactivity; ii) correct balancing of the decay equations; and iii) understanding of the mode of operation of the different radiation detectors.

Assess learners’ written products while looking for: i) coherence in the derivation of expression N = N₀e^(-λt) and its use to deduce an expression of half-life; ii) correct substitution in the decay equations to calculate the age of fossils and rocks; iii) ability to draw and explain the decay curve and use it to determine half-life of a radioactive material; and iv) correct statements for the hazards of radioisotopes and associated safety measures.
